title: The Regulative Principle of Worship
speaker: Pastor Jonathan Landry Cruze

outline.title: Definition and Distinction of the Regulative Principle
subpoints: The RPW states that God alone directs worship through His Word.
Only positive commands or necessary consequences from Scripture are permitted in corporate worship.
Contrasted with the Normative Principle, which permits anything not expressly forbidden.

outline.title: Historical Context in the Reformation
subpoints: The RPW was a hallmark of Reformed and Presbyterian worship.
The Westminster Assembly produced the Directory for Worship before the Confession.
The principle served to redress superstitious and idolatrous practices in Roman Catholic worship.

outline.title: Elements vs. Circumstances of Worship
subpoints: Elements are non-negotiable components commanded by Scripture (e.g., preaching, prayer, sacraments).
Circumstances are contextual details (e.g., time, attire) guided by the light of nature.
The distinction allows for flexibility in practice while maintaining doctrinal integrity.

outline.title: The Necessity of Defending the RPW
subpoints: Modern culture often views worship as subjective and personal.
Scripture presents worship as a serious matter where God cares about the manner.
The goal is to demonstrate that the RPW is not only right but supremely good.

outline.title: Argument from Scripture
subpoints: The Second Commandment specifically addresses the manner of worship.
Jesus’ teaching to the woman at the well emphasizes worship in spirit and truth.
Psalm 100 outlines the proper heart posture for worship.

summary:
In this Sunday school session, Pastor Jonathan Landry Cruze introduces the Regulative Principle of Worship (RPW) as a defining characteristic of Reformed and Presbyterian tradition. He defines the RPW as the belief that God alone directs how He is to be worshipped, and that this direction is found exclusively in His Word. The sermon contrasts this view with the Normative Principle, which permits any form of worship not expressly forbidden by Scripture. The pastor emphasizes that the RPW requires positive commands or necessary inferences from the Bible for corporate worship practices.

The discussion traces the historical roots of the RPW to the Reformation, noting that the Westminster Assembly’s Directory for Worship was the first document produced, establishing the principle as the chief guide for redressing superstitious practices. The sermon distinguishes between the 'elements' of worship, which are non-negotiable biblical commands such as preaching, prayer, and the sacraments, and the 'circumstances' of worship, which are contextual details like time and attire that can be guided by the light of nature.

Pastor Cruze argues that the RPW is necessary because modern culture often treats worship as subjective, assuming that only the heart matters. He asserts that Scripture presents worship as a serious matter where God cares deeply about the manner in which He is honored. The sermon outlines three arguments to defend the RPW: from Scripture, from doctrine, and from happiness, beginning with an examination of biblical texts such as the Second Commandment and Jesus’ teaching on true worship.
